weeks_data.topic: Information security fundamentals and risk management; SysInternals tools; Hyper-V lab environment; network and firewall setup

Monday.question: Which Week 1 area do you feel least prepared for right now?
options: Risk management fundamentals
Monitoring with SysInternals tools
Network and firewall configuration
Virtualization with Hyper-V

Tuesday.question: When inspecting a live Windows system with the Sysinternals Suite, which utility gives you the fastest insight into suspicious activity?
options: Process Explorer for parent-child process trees and loaded DLLs
Autoruns for persistence mechanisms across registry keys and scheduled tasks
TCPView for active network sockets and remote endpoints
Process Monitor (ProcMon) for real-time file, registry, and thread activity

Wednesday.question: When building a multi-VM lab in Hyper-V across physical hosts, which virtual switch or storage choice matters most?
options: External versus Internal versus Private virtual switch isolation
Static MAC and VLAN tagging on virtual network adapters
Fixed-size versus dynamically expanding VHDX performance and disk space
Checkpoints before making risky configuration changes

Thursday.question: When hardening host and perimeter firewall rules in Week 1, which mistake is most likely to break legitimate lab traffic?
options: Blocking required Active Directory, DNS, or SMB management ports
Confusing inbound versus outbound rule direction
Applying rules to the wrong Windows Firewall profile (Domain, Private, Public)
Leaving overly broad Any-to-Any allow rules active during testing

Friday.question: In foundational risk management, how do you decide whether to mitigate, transfer, avoid, or accept an identified operational risk?
options: Comparing mitigation cost against annualized loss expectancy and asset criticality
Mitigating high-likelihood, high-impact technical vulnerabilities first
Transferring catastrophic financial exposure through cyber insurance or SLAs
Requiring formal executive sign-off whenever residual risk is accepted

weeks_data.topic: Organizational readiness and planning; business impact analysis; threat assessment; diagramming for IR and DR planning

Monday.question: Which step do you think matters most in organizational readiness planning?
options: Business impact analysis
Threat and risk assessment
Diagramming the organization
Not sure yet

Tuesday.question: When conducting a Business Impact Analysis (BIA), what is the key difference between Recovery Time Objective (RTO) and Recovery Point Objective (RPO)?
options: RTO measures maximum tolerable downtime while RPO measures maximum tolerable data loss in time
RPO dictates backup and replication frequency
RTO dictates how quickly failover and system restoration must complete
Maximum Tolerable Downtime (MTD) sets the hard ceiling that RTO cannot exceed

Wednesday.question: During a threat and risk assessment for IR/DR readiness, which threat category is hardest to quantify accurately?
options: Targeted ransomware or supply-chain compromise
Insider threats and accidental administrative misconfiguration
Regional power, ISP, or cloud provider outages
Hardware failure on aging single-point-of-failure systems

Thursday.question: Why are accurate network and data-flow diagrams essential before an incident or outage occurs?
options: Responders cannot isolate or recover dependencies they do not know exist
Shows upstream and downstream blast radius when a core server or VLAN goes down
Identifies trust boundaries, firewall enforcement points, and external connections
Speeds up onboarding of external IR retainers or backup administrators during a crisis

Friday.question: When mapping critical business processes to underlying IT assets in Week 2, which hidden dependency is most often missed?
options: Core identity and DNS services (Active Directory, MFA, certificate authorities)
Third-party SaaS APIs and external authentication providers
Service accounts and scheduled batch jobs running on legacy servers
Physical facility dependencies like HVAC, generator fuel, and badge access

weeks_data.topic: Disaster recovery and business continuity planning; RAID and storage; backup and recovery; replication and failover; testing the plan

Monday.question: Which recovery element do you think is most often overlooked?
options: Testing backups
Replication and failover
Keeping the plan up to date
RAID and storage design

Tuesday.question: Why is RAID (such as RAID 1, RAID 5, RAID 6, or RAID 10) never a substitute for offline or immutable backups?
options: RAID immediately replicates ransomware encryption, file deletion, and logical corruption across drives
RAID only protects against physical disk failure within the same chassis or array
RAID 5 rebuilds on large drives risk a second drive failure during reconstruction
A site-level fire, flood, or power surge destroys the entire RAID array at once

Wednesday.question: When comparing full, incremental, and differential backup schedules, what is the main trade-off between backup speed and restore speed?
options: Incremental backups are fastest to write and use the least storage but require chaining the last full plus every incremental to restore
Differential backups require only the last full plus the latest differential to restore
Full backups are fastest to restore standalone but take the longest time and storage window
The 3-2-1-1-0 backup rule adds an air-gapped or immutable copy and zero unverified restore errors

Thursday.question: When choosing between cold site, warm site, and hot site recovery models, what drives the decision for each tier of applications?
options: Aligning site cost with the application's BIA Recovery Time Objective (RTO) and Recovery Point Objective (RPO)
Synchronous replication achieves near-zero RPO over short distances
Asynchronous replication balances WAN bandwidth cost with a small RPO window
Automated failover requires careful split-brain prevention and DNS/BGP cutover testing

Friday.question: When testing a Disaster Recovery plan, how does a tabletop walkthrough compare to a full parallel or failover test?
options: Tabletop exercises validate decision logic and roles safely, while failover tests prove actual technical recovery times
Simulation tests uncover missing credentials, expired certificates, and undocumented firewall rules
Untested backups frequently fail during a real disaster due to broken restore dependencies
Every DR test should produce a prioritized remediation list with owners and deadlines

weeks_data.topic: Incident response planning; escalation and communication; CSIRT organization and roles; Veeam backup and recovery

Monday.question: Which incident response team role do you expect to be hardest to fill?
options: Incident commander
Forensics analyst
Communications lead
Technical responder

Tuesday.question: In an Incident Response Plan aligned with NIST SP 800-61, why must severity classification and escalation thresholds be defined in advance?
options: Prevents on-call analysts from hesitating or under-escalating during the critical first hour
Clarifies when executive leadership, legal counsel, and external retainers must be paged
Matches response staffing and containment authority to business impact
Prevents alert fatigue from treating minor events as full-scale crises

Wednesday.question: During a live security incident, why is out-of-band communication critical for the CSIRT?
options: An attacker who compromised Active Directory or corporate email can monitor in-band Slack, Teams, and email channels
If primary infrastructure goes down during containment, corporate communication tools may be unreachable
Pre-established contact trees and encrypted out-of-band channels prevent confusion during an outage
Single-voice communication through the Communications Lead prevents conflicting updates to stakeholders

Thursday.question: When configuring Veeam Backup & Replication in the lab, which capability is most valuable for rapid service restoration?
options: Instant VM Recovery mounting a backup image directly to the hypervisor while storage migrates in the background
Application-aware processing (VSS) ensuring consistent Active Directory and SQL database state
SureBackup automated verification booting backups in an isolated virtual lab
Hardened immutable Linux repositories protecting backup chains from ransomware deletion

Friday.question: When restoring a domain controller or production server from a Veeam backup after an incident, what risk must you check before reconnecting it to the network?
options: Restoring a backup taken after the attacker established persistence re-introduces the backdoor
Active Directory non-authoritative versus authoritative restore and USN rollback prevention
Scanning restored images in an isolated quarantine VLAN before production cutover
Verifying post-restore service health, DNS registration, and trust relationships

weeks_data.topic: Incident detection strategies; SIEM; log analysis and forensic investigation; threat hunting

Monday.question: Which detection approach do you expect to rely on most in practice?
options: SIEM log correlation
Log analysis
Threat hunting
Continuous monitoring

Tuesday.question: Why is NTP time synchronization across all servers, firewalls, and endpoints a mandatory prerequisite for SIEM log correlation?
options: Skewed timestamps make it impossible to reconstruct an accurate timeline of lateral movement across hosts
Correlation rules rely on matching events within tight time windows
Forensic timelines lose evidentiary credibility if system clocks drift without documented offsets
Standardizing logs on UTC avoids daylight saving time and multi-timezone confusion

Wednesday.question: When analyzing Windows Security Event Logs during an investigation, which Event ID group gives you the clearest signal of credential abuse or persistence?
options: 4624 and 4625 (successful and failed logons, especially Logon Type 3 network and Type 10 RDP)
4688 and Sysmon Event ID 1 (process creation with full command-line arguments)
4697 / 7045 (new service installation) and 4698 (scheduled task creation)
1102 (audit log cleared by an administrator or attacker)

Thursday.question: How does hypothesis-driven threat hunting differ from waiting for automated SIEM or EDR alerts?
options: Threat hunters proactively search telemetry for adversary tradecraft (TTPs) that bypassed existing detection rules
Uses MITRE ATT&CK techniques to form testable hypotheses against historical logs
Successful hunts are converted into new automated SIEM detection rules
Reduces attacker dwell time before an adversary triggers noisy ransomware deployment

Friday.question: In comparing signature/indicator-based detection (IOCs) with behavioral detection (TTPs) on the Pyramid of Pain, why are behavioral detections more durable?
options: Attackers trivially change file hashes, IP addresses, and domains, but changing core TTPs is costly
Behavioral rules catch living-off-the-land binaries (LOLBins) like PowerShell and WMI abuse
IOC feeds remain useful for fast retrospective sweeps of known campaigns
Combining baseline anomaly detection with high-fidelity TTP rules balances false positives

weeks_data.topic: Splunk log collection and analysis; detection rules and alert tuning; containment, eradication and response strategies

Monday.question: Which containment step would you take first during a live incident?
options: Isolate the affected host
Disable compromised accounts
Block malicious traffic
Capture evidence first

Tuesday.question: When writing Splunk Search Processing Language (SPL) queries during an investigation, which command pattern do you find most useful?
options: stats count values() by ... to aggregate activity across users, hosts, and source IPs
timechart and bin to spot brute-force spikes or beaconing intervals over time
eval and rex to extract custom fields and classify suspicious command strings
lookup and subsearches to enrich events with asset criticality or threat intel

Wednesday.question: Why is alert tuning (reducing false positives while preserving true positives) one of the most important jobs in a SOC?
options: High false-positive rates cause analyst alert fatigue and lead to real intrusions being ignored
Suppressing noisy benign service accounts or vulnerability scanners sharpens signal quality
Adding contextual enrichment (asset owner, privilege level, geo-IP) speeds up triage
Testing detection rules against atomic attack simulations verifies true-positive coverage

Thursday.question: Why is it dangerous to immediately wipe and reimage a compromised server before completing scoping and containment?
options: Destroys volatile memory and disk evidence needed to determine how the attacker got in
Tips off the adversary while they still control other unmonitored hosts in the environment
Leaves the root vulnerability or stolen credentials active so the rebuilt server gets compromised again
Short-term network isolation (EDR host containment or VLAN quarantine) stops spread while preserving evidence

Friday.question: During the eradication phase, what must happen alongside removing malware and backdoors before systems return to production?
options: Rotating compromised credentials, Kerberos tickets (krbtgt), API keys, and certificates
Patching the initial-access vulnerability or closing the exposed management service
Auditing Active Directory for unauthorized domain admin accounts, GPO changes, or scheduled tasks
Heightened SIEM monitoring on recovered segments to confirm the adversary does not regain access

weeks_data.topic: Recovery, maintenance and investigation; forensic evidence handling; root cause analysis; after-action review

Monday.question: Which part of an after-action review do you think is most valuable?
options: Root cause analysis
Lessons learned
Evidence handling
Verifying recovery

Tuesday.question: When collecting digital forensic evidence from a compromised host, why must you follow the Order of Volatility (RFC 3227)?
options: RAM, active network connections, and running processes vanish as soon as power is pulled
Disk images and remote SIEM logs persist longer than volatile memory
Calculating SHA-256 cryptographic hashes proves acquired evidence was not altered
Maintaining a signed Chain of Custody log is required if evidence is used in legal or regulatory proceedings

Wednesday.question: When performing a Root Cause Analysis (such as the 5 Whys or Fishbone diagram) after an outage or breach, what is the biggest trap to avoid?
options: Stopping at human error instead of fixing the process or control gap that allowed the error
Confusing the triggering symptom with the underlying systemic vulnerability
Blaming individuals instead of running a blameless post-mortem that encourages honest reporting
Failing to trace why existing detection controls did not catch the issue earlier

Thursday.question: When bringing recovered systems back into production during Week 7, what validation step confirms the recovery is genuinely complete?
options: Verifying business application functionality, data integrity, and end-user workflows
Confirming backup agents, EDR sensors, and SIEM log forwarders are reporting cleanly
Running vulnerability and configuration compliance scans on the restored hosts
Monitoring performance metrics and security alerts closely through a post-recovery watch period

Friday.question: What separates an effective After-Action Review (AAR) from a report that sits on a shelf and changes nothing?
options: Turning each lesson learned into a specific engineering task with an assigned owner and due date
Updating the Incident Response Plan, runbooks, and SIEM rules based on what actually happened
Tracking metrics like Mean Time to Detect (MTTD) and Mean Time to Respond (MTTR)
Sharing an executive summary with leadership to justify security and resilience investments

weeks_data.topic: Disaster recovery plan and business continuity plan; recovery strategies and technical redundancy; communication planning

Monday.question: Which part of a DR or BC plan do you think is the biggest risk to get wrong?
options: Recovery priorities
Communication plan
Technical redundancy
Testing schedule

Tuesday.question: How do a Business Continuity Plan (BCP) and a Disaster Recovery Plan (DRP) complement each other during a major disruption?
options: BCP keeps essential business operations and people functioning while DRP restores IT infrastructure and data
BCP covers alternate workspaces, manual workarounds, and customer operations
DRP focuses on technical runbooks for servers, networks, storage, and applications
Both rely on the same Business Impact Analysis (BIA) recovery tiering

Wednesday.question: When designing technical redundancy, why does eliminating Single Points of Failure (SPOFs) require looking beyond just server hardware?
options: Redundant servers still fail together if they share one power feed, top-of-rack switch, storage array, or ISP
Geographic diversity protects against regional natural disasters and grid failures
Active-active load balancing requires database state synchronization across sites
DNS TTLs and BGP routing policies determine how fast external users fail over

Thursday.question: Why should a DRP order system restoration in strict dependency tiers (Tier 0 infrastructure before Tier 1 applications)?
options: Applications cannot start if core networking, DNS, Active Directory, and storage are not online first
Prevents recovery teams from competing for bandwidth and hypervisor resources simultaneously
Gives leadership predictable milestone checkpoints during a multi-hour restoration
Ensures security controls and logging are online before customer-facing services open

Friday.question: In a crisis communication plan, why do internal teams, customers, regulators, and media require separate communication templates?
options: Each audience needs a different level of technical detail, action items, and legal review
Internal staff need clear operational instructions and status updates
Customers need transparent impact scope, workarounds, and estimated resolution windows
Regulators and legal counsel require verified facts within statutory reporting deadlines

weeks_data.topic: Business continuity operations; supply chain resilience and vendor management; current threat landscape

Monday.question: Which continuity risk do you think organizations underestimate most?
options: Third-party vendor dependencies
Loss of facilities or power
Staff availability
Not sure yet

Tuesday.question: When evaluating third-party SaaS and supply-chain vendors for operational resilience, which question is most revealing?
options: What are the vendor's contractual SLA, RTO/RPO commitments, and breach notification timelines?
Does the vendor have SOC 2 Type II or ISO 27001 attestation and tested DR results?
How much privileged network or identity access does the vendor have into your environment?
What is your exit strategy or manual fallback if that vendor goes offline for a week?

Wednesday.question: Why have modern ransomware groups shifted from simple encryption to double and triple extortion?
options: Well-prepared organizations can restore from immutable backups without paying for a decryptor
Exfiltrating sensitive data before encryption adds regulatory and reputational pressure
Targeting MSPs, software supply chains, and hypervisors maximizes downstream impact
Zero-day exploitation of edge VPNs and firewalls bypasses traditional perimeter defenses

Thursday.question: During a prolonged outage or cyber incident, how do you protect against human-factor failure and key-person dependency?
options: Cross-training engineers and writing runbooks that any qualified responder can follow
Enforcing shift rotations during multi-day incidents to prevent burnout mistakes
Maintaining offline break-glass credentials so recovery does not depend on one unavailable admin
Running periodic exercises where the primary architect must observe without touching the keyboard

Friday.question: How does threat intelligence about the current threat landscape feed directly into Week 9 continuity operations?
options: Prioritizes patching and virtual shielding for vulnerabilities actively exploited in your sector
Updates tabletop scenarios to reflect real adversary playbooks (for example identity and backup targeting)
Identifies fourth-party concentration risks shared across critical suppliers
Guides network segmentation between vendor access zones and crown-jewel assets

weeks_data.topic: Crisis management; executive decision-making; stakeholder communication; international standards and regulation; building a resilient IR program

Monday.question: Which crisis management area do you expect to be most challenging?
options: Executive decision-making
Stakeholder communication
International standards and compliance
Building a resilient program

Tuesday.question: When briefing executive leadership during a high-stakes crisis, what do decision-makers need most from technical responders?
options: Clear business impact, verified facts versus assumptions, and concrete options with trade-offs
Translating technical indicators into operational, financial, and legal risk
Honest confidence levels and a committed time for the next status update
Guidance on critical trade-offs such as taking revenue systems offline to stop data exfiltration

Wednesday.question: How do frameworks and regulations like NIST CSF 2.0, ISO 27001/22301, GDPR, HIPAA, and SEC disclosure rules shape incident response?
options: Mandate strict breach notification timelines (such as 72 hours under GDPR or 4 business days for SEC material incidents)
NIST CSF 2.0 adds Govern alongside Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, and Recover
Require documented evidence of due care, risk assessments, and incident logs
Align technical security operations with board-level governance and audit accountability

Thursday.question: When measuring the maturity of an organization's Incident Response and Disaster Recovery program over time, which indicator shows real progress?
options: Declining Mean Time to Detect (MTTD) and Mean Time to Recover (MTTR) across drills and real incidents
100% of Tier 1 systems meeting their target RTO and RPO during unannounced recovery tests
Proactive closure of post-incident action items before the next quarterly review
Strong collaboration between IT ops, security, legal, and business unit owners

Friday.question: Looking back across all 10 weeks of BIT360, which capability do you feel most confident applying in a real operations or security role?
options: Monitoring, log analysis, and incident detection (Sysinternals, Windows Logs, SIEM/Splunk)
Designing and testing backups, replication, and Veeam recovery to meet RTO/RPO
Writing and executing structured Incident Response and Disaster Recovery plans
Leading root cause analysis, forensic evidence handling, and crisis communication
